newsitem.title: INDIA: IOC budget assumes India oil price rise.
newsitem.headline: IOC budget assumes India oil price rise.

text.p: Indian Oil Corp's 1997/98 (April-May) budget assumes the government will sanction a rise in state-controlled domestic refined product prices, the Economic Times daily reported on Sunday.
State-controlled IOC is the main distributing agency of refined products, some of which are sold to Indian consumers at heavily subsidised prices.
IOC, Oil and Natural Gas Corp, Hindustan Petroleum Corp Ltd and Bharat Petroleum Corp Ltd are owed around 160 billion ($4.4 billion) by the government for selling at subsidised prices.
Money owed to IOC accounts for around two thirds of the total oil pool deficit.
"A hike in the prices of petroleum products has already been worked into Indian Oil Corporation's budget for 1997/98," the Economic Times said.
The IOC budget plan shows the company counting on 14.06 billion rupees of internal resource accruals in 1997/98 and no external commercial borrowings.

This is a reverse picture from 1996/97. The company's revised estimates showed it failed to raise a single rupee from internal resource accruals and made external borrowings totalling 19.70 billion rupees.
The Economic Times said IOC had also substantially raised its total resource mobilisation target to 23.01 billion rupees in 1997/98 from 19.70 billion in 1996/97.

The IOC originally planned total resource mobilisation of 26.19 billion rupees, but because of the severe liquidity problems caused by the burgeoning oil pool deficit the company pared back its plans, and even then the toal bill was met from borrowings.
IOC officials could not be reached for comment.
Analysts expect the government to announce a hike in petroleum product prices in the coming weeks or soon after the start of the new fiscal year in April.
The government last raised prices in July, when it had only been in power a month, but that adjustment was soon rendered inadequate by a surge in world prices to six year highs.
The subsequent delay in raising prices again has caused the oil deficit to reach worrying proportions.
